WITH imp AS (                          -- the latest load of each pin-day
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (pin_id, impression_date) pin_id, impression_date, impressions
  FROM pin_daily_impressions
  ORDER BY pin_id, impression_date, loaded_at DESC
), imp_week AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', i.impression_date)::date AS week_start,
         p.pin_format,
         SUM(i.impressions) AS impressions
  FROM imp i
  JOIN pins p ON p.pin_id = i.pin_id
  GROUP BY 1, 2
), pairs AS (                          -- each (pin, pinner) once, at its first save
  SELECT pin_id, pinner_id, MIN(saved_at) AS first_saved_at
  FROM saves
  GROUP BY pin_id, pinner_id
), savers AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', s.first_saved_at)::date AS week_start,
         p.pin_format,
         COUNT(*) AS pin_savers
  FROM pairs s
  JOIN pins p ON p.pin_id = s.pin_id
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT w.week_start, w.pin_format, w.impressions,
       COALESCE(s.pin_savers, 0) AS pin_savers,
       ROUND(1000 * COALESCE(s.pin_savers, 0)::numeric / w.impressions, 2) AS savers_per_1k
FROM imp_week w
LEFT JOIN savers s ON s.week_start = w.week_start AND s.pin_format = w.pin_format
ORDER BY w.week_start, w.pin_format;

Explanation. The two inputs live at different grains (pin-day counts and individual saves), so each is aggregated to (week, format) on its own and then joined; joining saves to daily impression rows first would multiply both sides. Savers are pairs: grouping saves by (pin_id, pinner_id) collapses a pinner's several boards into one row, and taking MIN(saved_at) makes the pair belong to the week of its first save, which is the Hard rule (below Hard every pair's saves fall in one week, so it changes nothing). The impression side starts from the format-weeks, and a LEFT JOIN keeps formats that earned no savers, with COALESCE to 0. DISTINCT ON … ORDER BY loaded_at DESC keeps one load per pin-day (a no-op below Very Hard). With the session in UTC, date_trunc('week', …) returns the Monday.

Complexity. One sort or hash aggregate over saves, one over impression rows, and a small join: O(n log n) at worst. At scale, the first-save state is a table keyed by (pin, pinner) updated incrementally, and the weekly counts come from it.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(DATE(saved_at), WEEK(MONDAY)) (plain WEEK starts on Sunday); QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pin_id, impression_date ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) = 1 instead of DISTINCT ON; ROUND on NUMERIC rounds half away from zero, on FLOAT64 it is not guaranteed for binary halves. Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('week', …) follows the WEEK_START session parameter (default Monday semantics only with 0 or 1), QUALIFY again. Spark SQL: date_trunc('week', …) is Monday-based; no DISTINCT ON. MySQL 8: no DATE_TRUNC; use DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY).

Edge cases built into the data. A pinner who saves one pin to three boards on the same day; a pinner who saves two different pins of the same format in the same week; one format whose pins have impressions and no saves in a week (every level). Hard: two weeks; saves at Sunday 23:59:59 and Monday 00:00:00 UTC; pairs saved again in a later week; a second pinner whose first save is Monday 00:00:00. Very Hard: pin-days loaded two or three times with different counts.

Common mistakes. COUNT(*) of saves; COUNT(DISTINCT pinner_id) per format (undercounts pinners who save several pins); joining saves to daily impressions before aggregating (inflated impressions); an inner join that drops zero-saver formats; counting a pair in every week it was saved; summing every load; Sunday-based weeks; integer division (1000 * savers / impressions with integers truncates).

Follow-up guidance. (1) LAG(savers_per_1k) OVER (PARTITION BY pin_format ORDER BY week_start); the first week has no previous value (NULL, not 0), and a missing week for a format makes LAG compare non-adjacent weeks unless the weeks are densified first. (4) Track which pin-days each load touched, recompute only the affected weeks, and keep a restatement log with the week, old and new value, shown as a footnote on the chart.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH s AS (
  SELECT search_id, pinner_id, entry_point, source_pin_id, searched_at,
         LEAD(searched_at) OVER (PARTITION BY pinner_id ORDER BY searched_at) AS next_searched_at
  FROM visual_searches
), judged AS (
  SELECT s.entry_point,
         date_trunc('week', s.searched_at)::date AS week_start,
         EXISTS (
           SELECT 1
           FROM pin_actions a
           WHERE a.pinner_id = s.pinner_id
             AND a.action IN ('save', 'closeup')
             AND a.action_ts >= s.searched_at
             AND a.action_ts <= s.searched_at + INTERVAL '10 minutes'
             AND (s.next_searched_at IS NULL OR a.action_ts < s.next_searched_at)
             AND a.pin_id IS DISTINCT FROM s.source_pin_id
         ) AS ok
  FROM s
)
SELECT week_start, entry_point,
       COUNT(*)                     AS searches,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ok)   AS successful_searches,
       ROUND((COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ok))::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS success_rate
FROM judged
GROUP BY week_start, entry_point
ORDER BY week_start, entry_point;

Explanation. Success is a property of a search, so it is decided once per search with a correlated EXISTS: same pinner, a save or closeup, at or after the search and at most ten minutes after it. EXISTS stops at the first qualifying action, so a search followed by several actions is still one search, which is the most common trap. LEAD gives each search the pinner's next search; an action at or after it belongs to that later search (Hard). IS DISTINCT FROM excludes actions on the crop's source pin and is NULL-safe for camera and upload searches, whose source_pin_id is NULL (Very Hard; below that level no action targets a source pin, so the condition changes nothing). The week comes from searched_at, so a Sunday-night search that succeeds after midnight stays in its own week.

Complexity. One window sort of searches by pinner and time, and for each search an index range lookup on pin_actions (pinner_id, action_ts): O(s log a). Without that index the planner may hash-join on pinner and filter, still fine at this size.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: correlated EXISTS is supported but often rewritten as a join on pinner with a time filter and LOGICAL_OR; TIMESTAMP_ADD(searched_at, INTERVAL 10 MINUTE); DATE_TRUNC(DATE(searched_at), WEEK(MONDAY)). Snowflake: DATEADD(minute, 10, searched_at), BOOLOR_AGG over a left join; IS DISTINCT FROM exists. Spark SQL: EXISTS subqueries are supported in WHERE but not always in SELECT; use a left semi join on a precomputed set of successful search ids. MySQL 8: LEAD, EXISTS and DATE_ADD(…, INTERVAL 10 MINUTE); no IS DISTINCT FROM, use NOT (a.pin_id <=> s.source_pin_id).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a search with a closeup and a save; an action at exactly +10:00 and one at +10:01; an action before the search only; an outbound click only; a save by another pinner just after a search; searches with nothing after them. Hard: a pinner's second search a few minutes after the first, with the action after the second (it belongs to the second only); an action at exactly the second search's time; a Sunday 23:5x search whose save comes after Monday 00:00 UTC. Very Hard: crop searches whose only action is on the source pin, and one with an action on the source pin and a save of another pin.

Common mistakes. COUNT(*) after a join to actions (rates above 1); BETWEEN with a strict upper bound, or < at 10 minutes; ABS(action_ts - searched_at) <= 10 minutes (actions before the search); counting outbound clicks; not cutting at the next search, or cutting with <=; source_pin_id <> pin_id, which is NULL for camera and upload searches and silently drops all of them; the week of the action instead of the search.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Take the first qualifying action per search with MIN(action_ts) in a lateral or grouped join, then PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY seconds); searches with no save are censored, so report the median among successful searches together with the success rate, never instead of it. (2) Plot the share of first actions by minute after the search; choose the knee and test 5, 10 and 20 minutes; report whether the ranking of entry points is stable across them. (3) Stratify by device or platform (or compare the same pinners across entry points); the raw comparison mixes intent and device. (4) Keep per pinner the open searches of the last 10 minutes (at most a few), keyed by pinner in the stream; an action closes the latest open search; emit each search's outcome when its window closes, with event time and a lateness bound.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but join rows counted, or one boundary wrong. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains why the proxy is a proxy and how to compute it in a stream.

Strong signals. Asks which actions count and whether the bound is inclusive; uses EXISTS deliberately; mentions the NULL trap with source pins. Red flags. Proposing to store or analyse the searched image or infer anything about the pinner from it; treating the proxy as ground truth.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{fresh_days}} is the instance's window)

WITH imp AS (                          -- a retried log is one impression
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (impression_id) impression_id, pin_id, country, impression_ts
  FROM home_feed_impressions
  ORDER BY impression_id, log_id
), aged AS (
  SELECT (i.impression_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS impression_date,
         i.country,
         i.impression_ts < COALESCE(o.published_at, o.created_at)
                           + INTERVAL '{{fresh_days}} days' AS fresh
  FROM imp i
  JOIN pins p ON p.pin_id = i.pin_id
  JOIN pins o ON o.pin_id = COALESCE(p.original_pin_id, p.pin_id)   -- the original
)
SELECT impression_date, country,
       COUNT(*)                        AS impressions,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE fresh)   AS fresh_impressions,
       ROUND((COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE fresh))::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS fresh_share
FROM aged
GROUP BY impression_date, country
ORDER BY impression_date, country;

Explanation. Each impression is joined twice to pins: once for the shown pin, once for its original, chosen with COALESCE(original_pin_id, pin_id) so originals join to themselves. The age is measured from the original's start (its publish time if scheduled, otherwise its creation; below Very Hard published_at is always NULL), and the comparison is written as impression_ts < start + interval, so the boundary is exclusive by construction. DISTINCT ON (impression_id) removes the client's retried logs before anything is counted (below Hard it is a no-op). With the session in UTC, adding 'N days' is exactly N × 24 hours, and AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' gives the UTC date.

Complexity. A sort or hash for the dedupe, two hash joins to pins and a hash aggregate: O(n log n) at worst over the log. At scale, storing each pin's original start on the pin row (denormalised at write time) removes the second join.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY impression_id ORDER BY log_id) = 1; TIMESTAMP_ADD(start, INTERVAL n DAY) (always 24-hour days on TIMESTAMP); COUNTIF. Snowflake: DATEADD(day, n, start) on TIMESTAMP_TZ keeps the offset; QUALIFY; COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: start + make_interval(0, 0, 0, n) or timestampadd(DAY, n, start); count_if. MySQL 8: DATE_ADD(start, INTERVAL n DAY) on DATETIME (no zone, so store UTC); no DISTINCT ON, use ROW_NUMBER in a CTE.

Edge cases built into the data. Repins created minutes or hours before the day of old originals (every level, each shown at least once); originals a few days too old and long ago; an impression exactly N days after an original's creation (not fresh) and one of its repin a second earlier (fresh). Hard: two UTC days with impressions at 23:59:59 and 00:00:00; some impressions logged twice. Very Hard: a scheduled pin created long before the window and published inside it, a repin of it, and one published just before the window that ages out during the data.

Common mistakes. Using the shown pin's created_at (the repin trap); <= or BETWEEN at the boundary; impression_ts::date - created_at::date < N (whole calendar days, not 24-hour periods); counting log rows instead of impressions, or deduping the total but not the fresh count; created_at instead of the publish time for scheduled pins; dates in a non-UTC session zone.

Follow-up guidance. (1) COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.original_pin_id IS NOT NULL); a repin share measures how much of the feed is re-circulation, which overlaps with but is not the same as staleness (a fresh original can be repinned within the hour). (2) A chain needs the root: a recursive CTE per query is expensive at scale; better to store root_pin_id on each pin when the repin is created (a write-time lookup of one row). (3) Define relevance by aggregate signals (saves of the pin in the last weeks across all pinners, season-over-season interest) rather than by any individual's history; report both "fresh by creation" and "recently resurging" as separate aggregates. (4) Denormalise the original's start onto the impression at logging or in a daily enrichment that reads only the pins seen that day (a semi-join on the day's distinct pin ids), partition the log by date, and keep the result as a per-day, per-country aggregate.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but repins dated by themselves, or the boundary inclusive. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles chains and scale with a stored root, and keeps the measure aggregate.

Strong signals. Restates the repin rule before writing SQL; writes the window as an exclusive upper bound; checks for duplicate impression ids unprompted. Red flags. Treating the measure as an input to ranking individuals; inferring anything about viewers from what they were shown.

from bisect import bisect_left


def distinct_savers(saves, queries):
    by_pin = {}
    for pin, day, who in saves:
        by_pin.setdefault(pin, []).append((day, who))
    asks = {}
    for qi, (pin, first, last) in enumerate(queries):
        if first <= last and pin in by_pin:              # everything else stays 0
            asks.setdefault(pin, []).append((last, first, qi))
    out = [0] * len(queries)
    for pin, qs in asks.items():
        ev = by_pin[pin]
        ev.sort(key=lambda e: e[0])                      # saves by day
        days = sorted({d for d, _ in ev})
        pos = {d: i + 1 for i, d in enumerate(days)}     # Fenwick index of each distinct day
        n = len(days)
        tree = [0] * (n + 1)
        latest = {}                                      # pinner -> latest save day swept so far
        qs.sort()                                        # by last_day
        j, m = 0, len(ev)
        for last, first, qi in qs:
            while j < m and ev[j][0] <= last:
                d, who = ev[j]
                j += 1
                prev = latest.get(who)
                if prev == d:
                    continue
                if prev is not None:                     # move the pinner's mark to day d
                    i = pos[prev]
                    while i <= n:
                        tree[i] -= 1
                        i += i & -i
                i = pos[d]
                while i <= n:
                    tree[i] += 1
                    i += i & -i
                latest[who] = d
            i, before = bisect_left(days, first), 0      # marks on days < first
            while i > 0:
                before += tree[i]
                i -= i & -i
            out[qi] = len(latest) - before
    return out

Explanation. Distinct counts are not additive, so prefix counts cannot be subtracted. The offline trick: answer queries in order of last_day while sweeping saves in day order, and keep exactly one mark per pinner, on the day of their latest save so far. After sweeping every save up to last_day, a pinner saved within [first_day, last_day] if and only if their latest save so far is on a day ≥ first_day: if they saved in the range, their latest save is at least that day; if their latest save up to last_day is before first_day, they did not save in the range. So the answer is the number of marks on days ≥ first_day, which is the number of pinners seen minus the marks before first_day. Marks move, so the count needs point updates and prefix sums: a Fenwick tree over the distinct days, with bisect_left turning first_day into a prefix length (it works for days with no saves). Queries are grouped per pin, so pins never mix, and empty, reversed or unknown-pin queries stay 0.

Complexity. O(n log n + q log q + (n + q) log D) time for n saves, q queries and D distinct days, O(n + D) memory. The timing test (200 000 saves, 50 000 ranges, 3 000 days) runs in about 0.6–0.9 s in CPython. A set built per range took about 10 s for only 2 000 of the 50 000 ranges (several minutes in all). The most likely middle approach, unions of per-day pinner sets, is no better (each range still touches every day in it). Mo's algorithm, O((n + q)·√n), is a legitimate sublinear answer but took 11–15 s here, so it fails the test; credit the idea in discussion, not as a pass.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ the Fenwick tree is an int[] and the queries an array of indices sorted by right end; pinner ids should be interned to ints first. In SQL the same question is COUNT(DISTINCT pinner_id) with a range join of queries to saves (O(q·len) again), or a precomputed table of each pinner's first save per day for fixed ranges only. Spark: approximate per-day sketches (approx_count_distinct on HLL++ states) merged per range. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Repeat saves by one pinner in a range; both bounds inclusive; a one-day range; a range between saves (0); a pinner whose earlier save is in the range and later one is not; the same range asked twice and queries out of order. Hard: unsorted saves, many saves by one pinner on one day, first_day > last_day (0), ranges before or after all data (0). Very Hard: one pinner saving two pins (counted per pin), a pin with no saves (0), interleaved queries across pins.

Common mistakes. prefix(b) − prefix(a − 1) with distinct counts; marking a pinner's first save instead of the latest (then the sweep must be by left end, mirrored); forgetting to remove the previous mark; indexing the tree by raw day numbers without compression and off by one at day 0; returning answers in sorted order; mixing pins in one tree.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Invariant: after the sweep reaches last_day, each pinner seen has exactly one mark, on their latest save ≤ last_day; they saved in the range iff that mark is ≥ first_day. (2) Online: a persistent segment tree keeps one version per day (O(log D) new nodes per mark move); a query reads version last_day and counts marks ≥ first_day, O(log D) per query and O(n log D) memory. (3) Store an HLL sketch per pin per day; a range merges up to D sketches (or uses a sparse table of merged sketches for O(1) merges per query); relative error about 1.04/√m for m registers, and for small counts use exact sets (sparse representation). (4) A deletion removes a save; if it was the pinner's latest in a version, the mark moves back to their previous save; offline, recompute with the deleted rows filtered; decide with product whether "savers" means current or historical savers, and say so on the chart.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct small cases with a set per range, or a prefix-difference idea that fails on repeat savers. 3: all tests pass with the offline sweep and a Fenwick or segment tree. 4: also proves the invariant and handles online queries or sketches credibly.

Strong signals. Says early that distinct counts do not subtract; asks whether queries are offline; compresses the days. Red flags. Presenting an approximate count as exact; exposing who saved to the creator.

def busier_lookback(rows):
    per = {}
    for pin, day, saves in rows:                 # a day split over rows adds up
        d = per.setdefault(pin, {})
        d[day] = d.get(day, 0) + saves
    out = {}
    for pin, d in per.items():
        stack, res = [], []                      # (day, saves) with strictly decreasing saves
        for day in sorted(d):
            s = d[day]
            while stack and stack[-1][1] <= s:   # never busier than today, nor than any later day that beats today
                stack.pop()
            res.append(day - stack[-1][0] if stack else 0)
            stack.append((day, s))
        out[pin] = res
    return out

Explanation. For each day the answer is the previous strictly greater element. Once day j is followed by a day k with at least as many saves, j can never be the answer for any day after k: any later day that j beats, k beats too, and k is closer. So the candidates form a stack of strictly decreasing saves; each day pops the candidates it ties or beats (<=, because an equal day is not busier), reads the busier day from the top, and pushes itself. Each day is pushed and popped at most once. Grouping into a per-pin dict sums split days and makes row order irrelevant; sorting the days gives day order, and the difference of day numbers gives calendar days across gaps (a missing day had no saves, so it is never a candidate).

Complexity. O(n log n) for sorting each pin's days plus O(n) for the stack (O(n) overall if rows arrive sorted), O(n) memory. The timing test (100 pins × 3 000 days, 300 000 values) runs in about 0.1–0.6 s in CPython (the upper end with unordered rows to group and sort). Scanning back from each day took about 21–22 s on the same data, because most pins open with a launch spike and then climb with long plateaus, so the scan runs to day 1. import heapq


def price_drop_alerts(saves, prices, pct=90):
    # One sweep over days. On a day, price rows (kind 0) come before saves (kind 1),
    # so a save takes that day's price and can only alert on a later day.
    events = [(day, 0, product, price) for product, day, price in prices]
    events += [(day, 1, product, i) for i, (product, day) in enumerate(saves)]
    events.sort(key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1]))
    current = {}          # product -> price in force (None while out of stock)
    pending = {}          # product -> max-heap of (-pct * saved price, save index)
    out = [-1] * len(saves)
    for day, kind, product, x in events:
        if kind == 0:
            current[product] = x
            if x is None:
                continue                      # out of stock: nothing can alert today
            heap = pending.get(product)
            limit = 100 * x
            while heap and -heap[0][0] >= limit:
                out[heapq.heappop(heap)[1]] = day
        else:
            price = current.get(product)
            if price is not None:             # no price yet, or out of stock: never alerts
                heapq.heappush(pending.setdefault(product, []), (-pct * price, x))
    return out

Explanation. Each save becomes a pending threshold pct × saved price on its product. A later price p triggers every pending save of that product whose threshold is at least 100 × p. The pending saves with the highest thresholds trigger first, so a max-heap per product answers "who alerts today?" by popping from the top until the top no longer qualifies. Every save is pushed once and popped at most once. Sorting rows and saves together by (day, kind) with price rows first gives the two same-day rules in one place: a row dated the save day sets the saved price, and alerts only happen on later days. Because a price holds until the next row, the first qualifying day is always a row's day, so only rows need to be visited. An out-of-stock row updates the current price to None and pops nothing, and a save made while out of stock is never pushed.

Complexity. O((s + d) log(s + d)) for the sort, plus O(s log s) heap work, for s saves and d price rows. O(s + d) memory. The timing test (150 000 saves, 20 products, 4 000 days) runs in about 0.6 s in CPython. A forward scan per save, with a bisect to the save day first, takes about 16 to 25 s, depending on the level, because most saves stay pending for thousands of rows; that is 25 to 40 times slower and well over the 8 s limit.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution sweeps days correctly but keeps each product's pending saves in a plain list and checks the whole list on every price row. It is O(d · pending) and takes 25 to 55 s on the timing test, so it fails. A sorted list of thresholds per product with bisect.insort and popping from the high end is O(log s) comparisons and O(s) memory moves per insert in C. It passes comfortably and is an acceptable answer. So is a segment tree or sparse table of minimum prices per product, with a "first index after the save whose price is at most the threshold" descent per save, at O((s + d) log d).

Dialect notes. In Java use a PriorityQueue<long[]> per product with a reversed comparator, and long for pct × price (cents times 100 stays far from overflow, but say so). In SQL the per-save answer is a correlated MIN(day) over later rows with 100 * price <= pct * saved_price, joined to the as-of saved price. That is correct and set-based, but it is the same O(s·d) scan unless the engine can use an index on (product, day) with a price predicate it cannot range-scan. A warehouse would batch it per product and day, and an incremental daily run would keep pending thresholds in a table. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A price of exactly pct per cent (alerts); one cent above (does not); a cheaper row on the save day itself (sets the saved price, no alert); the first qualifying day rather than the cheapest; saves before the product's first row (-1); two saves measured against their own saved prices; a drop on another product; rows out of order and interleaved; two saves on the same day; a save on the last row's day; a product with no rows. Very Hard adds out-of-stock days that never alert, a return from out of stock at a low price (alerts that day), a save while out of stock, and a return above the threshold followed by a real drop.

Common mistakes. Alerting on the save day; using the first price after the save as the saved price; floating-point 0.9 * price instead of the integer rule; reporting the cheapest day; treating an out-of-stock row as price 0, which alerts every pending save; assuming rows are sorted; a min-heap of thresholds, which tests the wrong end; scanning each save forward.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Key pending alerts by (pinner, product). Keep the earliest save's price, or the lowest, and say which; the choice changes when pinners hear about a drop. (2) Keep the pending heaps (or a table of thresholds per product) between runs, and apply only the new day's rows. A product saved by millions of pinners needs its thresholds bucketed (all saves at the same saved price share one entry with a list or a count) and expired after a stated period. (3) Require the low price to hold for a stated time, or for two consecutive feed updates, and cap alerts per product per hour. A merchant's correction should cancel alerts not yet sent. (4) Comparing across currencies is meaningless. Store currency with every row and saved price, compare only like with like, and decide whether a currency change resets pending saves.

def discordant_pairs(shown, scores, report_comparable=False):
    seen = set()
    vals = []
    for pin in shown:
        if pin in seen:
            continue                          # a scroll-back: the first position counts
        seen.add(pin)
        s = scores.get(pin)
        if s is not None:
            vals.append(s)

    def count(a):
        # Sort a in descending order; return (sorted, pairs i < j with a[i] < a[j]).
        n = len(a)
        if n < 2:
            return a, 0
        left, cl = count(a[: n // 2])
        right, cr = count(a[n // 2:])
        merged = []
        put = merged.append
        i, ln, c = 0, len(left), cl + cr
        for x in right:
            while i < ln and left[i] >= x:    # ties: the left element goes first
                put(left[i])
                i += 1
            c += ln - i                       # left[i:] are earlier and strictly smaller
            put(x)
        merged.extend(left[i:])
        return merged, c

    discordant = count(vals)[1]
    if not report_comparable:
        return discordant
    groups = {}
    for v in vals:
        groups[v] = groups.get(v, 0) + 1
    m = len(vals)
    tied = sum(k * (k - 1) // 2 for k in groups.values())
    return (discordant, m * (m - 1) // 2 - tied)

Explanation. After dropping repeats and unscored pins, the shown order is a list of scores v. A discordant pair is i < j with v[i] < v[j], which is an inversion count for a descending sort. Merge sort each half into descending order. While merging, when a right element x is placed, every left element still waiting is smaller than x (they are below the last left element that was at least x), and each was shown earlier, so each forms one discordant pair. Taking the left element first on a tie means equal scores are never counted. Comparable pairs are all pairs minus the pairs inside each group of equal scores.

Complexity. O(n log n) time and O(n) memory; recursion depth is about log₂ n. The timing test (380 000 shown pins) runs in about 1.3 s in CPython, including the deduplication pass. A Fenwick tree over score ranks is also O(n log n) and takes about 2 to 2.5 s, inside the limit. Comparing all pairs is about 10¹¹ comparisons, many hours in CPython.

The middle approach, and what this sizing does to it. The likely middle answer keeps a sorted list of the scores seen so far, uses bisect to count the smaller ones and bisect.insort to add the new score. It makes only O(log n) comparisons per pin, but each insert shifts on average a quarter of the list in C, so it is O(n²) memory moves. On the timing test the scores are in random order relative to the shown order, so inserts land in the middle on average whichever direction the list is kept in. It takes about 10 s in CPython at 380 000 pins (about 15 s at 450 000 and 19 s at 500 000), roughly ten times the reference and about twice the 8 s limit, so it fails, though by a smaller factor than the pure O(n²) loop. On a much faster machine it could come close to the limit; the follow-up rule on insort is there so the interviewer asks for the move count either way. Expect a candidate who uses it to explain why it is quadratic despite the binary search.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ the count needs a 64-bit integer (long, int64_t): a reversed list of 380 000 pins has about 10¹¹ pairs. In SQL a self-join on pos_a < pos_b AND score_a < score_b is correct and O(n²). Engines with window functions cannot express the inversion count directly in O(n log n). In Spark, the usual approach is a per-list job in the driver or a UDF with the same merge sort, because lists are independent. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Shown in exactly the scoring order (0); exactly reversed (n(n−1)/2); one adjacent swap (1); one pin; nothing shown (0, or (0, 0) at Very Hard); negative scores; the last pin moved to the front. Hard and Very Hard add equal scores, every score equal, a repeated pin counted at its first position (two tests, including a pin that was low at first and repeated high), a pin with no score, and ties inside a reversed order.

Common mistakes. Counting the wrong direction; counting equal scores as discordant (taking the right element first on a tie); keeping a repeated pin's last position; crashing on an unscored pin (scores[pin]); computing comparable pairs as n(n−1)/2 without removing ties; a recursive merge sort that slices with list.pop(0), which is quadratic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Kendall's tau-b: (concordant − discordant) / √((n₀ − n₁)(n₀ − n₂)), where n₀ is all pairs and n₁, n₂ the tied pairs in each ordering. Here the shown order has no ties, so the denominator uses only the score ties. The Very Hard return gives what is needed. (2) Weight a pair by a function of the earlier position, for example 1 / log₂(position + 1). The merge sort can carry, for each left element, its weight, and add the sum of the remaining left weights, kept as a suffix sum, instead of their count. (3) Keep a Fenwick tree over score ranks for the window, adding pins as they are shown and removing them when they fall out of the window; each pin then costs O(log n). (4) Skipped pins are not missing at random if the sampling depends on position or score. Report the coverage with the number, or compute it on a uniform sample of pairs.

Rubric anchors. 2: an O(n²) loop or insort without seeing why it is slow, or the direction or ties wrong. 3: all tests pass with a merge sort or Fenwick tree and correct tie handling. 4: also explains the tie rule precisely, notes the 64-bit count, and handles the normalisation and position-weighting follow-ups.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

MIN_VIEW_MS = 2000              # a video view counts after 2 seconds watched (this exercise's rule)


def _original(pins, pin):
    while pins[pin]["origin"] is not None:      # follow the whole chain
        pin = pins[pin]["origin"]
    return pin


def _week(ts):
    day = datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc).date()          # weeks are cut in UTC
    return (day - timedelta(days=day.weekday())).isoformat()


def weekly_engagement(events, pins):
    rows = {}
    for ev in events:
        if ev["pin"] not in pins:
            continue
        root = _original(pins, ev["pin"])
        if pins[root]["deleted"]:                                    # the original decides
            continue
        t = ev["type"]
        metric = None
        if t == "impression":
            metric = "impressions"
        elif t == "save":
            if ev["board"] != "secret":                              # public and group boards count
                metric = "saves"
        elif t == "closeup":
            if pins[root]["format"] == "static":
                metric = "views"
        elif t == "video_view":
            if pins[root]["format"] == "video" and ev["watched_ms"] >= MIN_VIEW_MS:
                metric = "views"
        if metric:
            key = root + "|" + _week(ev["ts"])
            row = rows.setdefault(key, {"impressions": 0, "saves": 0, "views": 0})
            row[metric] += 1
    return rows

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Repins credited one hop up. _original returns the pin's origin without following it further. Symptom: engagement on a repin of a repin is credited to the middle pin, someone else's repin, instead of the original. Fix: follow origin until it is None.
  2. Group-board saves dropped. The save check is board == "public", so saves to group boards are dropped along with secret ones. Symptom: pins popular with group boards look less saved. Fix: exclude only "secret".
  3. Deletion checked on the wrong pin. The code skips events whose own pin is deleted. Symptom, two ways: a deleted repin's real saves and impressions disappear from the original, and a deleted original still gets rows through its live repins. Fix: resolve the original first and check its deleted flag.
  4. Units. watched_ms is compared with MIN_VIEW_SECONDS = 2, so every view of 2 ms or more counts. Symptom: video views far above the player's own numbers. Fix: compare milliseconds with 2 000.
  5. Weeks cut at UTC−8. REPORT_TZ_OFFSET shifts every timestamp eight hours back before the week is cut. Symptom: events between Monday 00:00 and 07:59 UTC land in the previous week, so weekly totals disagree with the UTC dashboards. Fix: cut weeks in UTC.

Each bug has its own check: a repin of a repin; a group-board save; a deleted repin and a deleted original (two checks); a short video view; an event early on Monday, and the Sunday 23:59:59 / Monday 00:00:00 pair. The other checks (a secret save, a 2-second view with a closeup on a video pin, an unknown pin, a one-hop repin) pass on the buggy code and stay as regression checks. Random samples can hit several bugs at once.

Explanation. The rollup is three decisions per event: which pin gets credit (the original, through the whole chain), whether the event counts (deleted original, secret board, view rules by format and units), and which week it belongs to (Monday in UTC). Each bug breaks exactly one of those decisions.

Complexity. O(n · chain length) time. The timing test (200 000 events, 20 000 pins, chains of a few levels) runs well under a second. A memo from pin to original makes it O(n + pins) and is the right answer to the long-chain follow-up.

Dialect notes. In SQL the original is a recursive CTE over origin, or better, an original_pin_id column computed when a repin is created. The week is date_trunc('week', ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') in PostgreSQL, which starts on Monday. In BigQuery DATE_TRUNC(d, WEEK) starts on Sunday unless you write WEEK(MONDAY) or ISOWEEK. Snowflake's DATE_TRUNC('week', …) depends on the WEEK_START session parameter. Spark's date_trunc('week', …) starts on Monday. Watch the session time zone in every engine. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Impressions and a closeup on one static pin; a one-hop repin; a repin of a repin; a secret save; a group save; a deleted repin; a deleted original reached through a live repin; a video view under 2 seconds; exactly 2 seconds, with a closeup on a video pin; an event in the first hours of Monday UTC; Sunday 23:59:59 against Monday 00:00:00; an event for an unknown pin.

Fixing the one-hop credit with two hops; changing the save check to in ("public", "group"), which works today and silently drops the next board type; moving the deleted check but still checking the event's pin as well, which drops the deleted repin's real engagement; changing the constant to 2000 but leaving the name MIN_VIEW_SECONDS; computing Sunday-start weeks while removing the offset; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes.

(2) Both answers are defensible: either restate history (the pin is gone) or keep an as-reported snapshot. Store the deletion time so both can be produced. (3) Partition by week and recompute whole partitions; call a week final after the stated lateness (three days), and mark earlier versions as provisional. (4) Store original_pin_id on each pin at creation (a repin copies its parent's original), so the rollup never walks a chain. Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • What exists where. The pinner's photo exists only in memory on the serving path: it is decoded, objects are detected, the query features are computed and the image is dropped when the response is sent. It is never written to logs, queues, caches with persistence, crash dumps or debug tables. Crash reporting on that path is configured to exclude request bodies.
  • Request event. visual_search_request (request_id, served_at, entry_point camera|crop_on_pin|upload, client, country, source_pin_id NULL, crop_box NULL, detections[{label, box, confidence}], model_version, result_count). request_id is random per search and expires after the {{followup_window}} join. source_pin_id and crop_box exist only for crops on public pins, because the image is then a public pin, not the pinner's photo. Detections come from a fixed list of object labels.
  • Results event. results_served (request_id, position, pin_id, is_product) per served result, or one row with an array. Deduplicated on (request_id, position).
  • Actions. Closeups, saves and outbound clicks from the results grid carry the request_id the server issued. A stream job joins actions to requests within the {{followup_window}} window, using event time with an allowed lateness, and writes visual_search_outcome (request_id, first_action, first_action_type, useful bool).
  • No pinner identifier. The log has no pinner id or device id. Questions that need repeat behaviour are out of scope for this log (follow-up 3).
  • Aggregates. Daily and weekly tables by entry point, object label, country and model version: searches, useful searches, useful rate, actions by type. Cells under a threshold (for example fewer than 100 searches) are suppressed, and totals are computed from unsuppressed cells or published with the suppressed remainder grouped.
  • Retention. Raw request, result and action events are kept for {{retention}} and deleted by partition, with a deletion job that verifies by listing and alerts on failure. Aggregates without request ids can be kept longer.
  • Proof. A schema test fails the build if any field in these tables holds bytes, base64 or a vector. A sampled scanner checks payloads for image signatures (JPEG/PNG headers, long base64 runs) and blocks the producer on a hit. Access to raw tables is logged.

Competing designs to accept. Logging only aggregates at the edge and nothing per request (accept if the candidate explains how the {{followup_window}} join is done in a short-lived in-memory window); keeping a per-request object list without boxes; a client-side join that sends only the outcome. All are fine if the photo and anything reversible from it never leave the serving path.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Debug convenience pulling images into logs; error events with payloads; embeddings treated as "not the image"; joins that need a pinner id; client retries duplicating results-served; late action events falling outside the window; silent retention failures.

Incident guidance.

  • A thumbnail in the error event for six hours: stop the producer (feature flag or schema rejection), delete the affected partitions and any downstream copies, verify by scanning, record what was deleted and who had access, and add the payload scanner and a schema rule that would have blocked it. Tell the privacy owner; this is a breach of the log's rule, not a data-quality issue.
  • Duplicate results-served events: deduplicate on (request_id, position) at ingestion or in the table, rerun the day's aggregates, and add a monitor on results per request.
  • Retention deletion failing for a week: alert on the age of the oldest partition, not on job success. Run the deletion for the backlog, verify, and fix the job to address partitions by date, not by name.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Use the logged labels, boxes, model versions and result ids to find patterns (low confidence for "chair", low useful rate); reproduce with consented test images or public pins, never with pinners' photos. (2) Detect with the payload scanner and schema checks; stop the release or reject the field at ingestion; delete the written data and verify. (3) It needs a stable pinner identifier, which this log deliberately lacks. Answer it from a separate, consented dataset with its own retention, or approximate it from aggregates; do not add a pinner id to this log. (4) Scale the stream join and partitioning; the new entry point needs the same rule that frames are never stored, and the scanner must cover video payloads.

Rubric anchors. 2: logs the image or an embedding "for debugging", or joins on pinner id. 3: a schema without the photo, a short-lived request id, a windowed join with late events, deduplication, aggregates and retention. 4: also small-cell suppression with protection against subtraction, automated proof that no image is kept, and a breach-grade response to the thumbnail incident.
