Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Save identity. The client mints a random save_id (a UUID) when the pinner taps save, and sends it with every retry. The save API creates the pin with save_id as an idempotency key: a unique constraint, or a lookup in a deduplication store with a window longer than the {{offline_hours}}-hour offline queue plus margin. A retry returns the existing pin.
  • Events. save_created, save_edited, save_deleted, each with save_id, pin_id, a per-save client_seq that the client increments, client_ts, server_received_at, client and version. The stream is partitioned by save_id, so all versions of one save are processed in order of arrival on one partition.
  • Applying out-of-order events. A record per save_id holds the latest state by client_seq, never by arrival. A delete writes a tombstone kept at least as long as the offline window, so a create that arrives after its delete stays deleted. An edit with a lower client_seq than the stored one is ignored.
  • Source page. The URL is normalised by a versioned rule: lower-case scheme and host, drop the fragment, drop known tracking parameters and anything that looks like a session token or credential, sort the remaining parameters. The raw URL is never stored. Keep source_domain, source_url_normalised and normalisation_version, so history can be re-normalised.
  • Save time. Keep client_ts and server_received_at. Use client_ts when it is within a plausible range (not after receipt, and not more than the offline window before it), otherwise use the receive time and flag the row. Reports state which rule they use.
  • Analytics table. external_saves (save_id, pin_id, save_date, save_time, time_source, client, source_domain, source_url_normalised, normalisation_version, deleted_at), partitioned by save_date. Late events rewrite the partition of their save date. A daily job rebuilds the last few days from the current record state, and deletions remove rows within a day. Creator views read aggregates by claimed domain and day, never rows.

Competing designs to accept. Server-minted ids with a client request id for retries; event sourcing with periodic snapshots; a CDC stream from the pin store instead of client events (accept if the candidate explains how the source page and client are captured). All are fine if retries are idempotent and deletes win over late creates.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Deduplication windows shorter than offline periods; ordering by arrival time; storing raw URLs with tokens; client clocks hours off; deleted pins lingering in analytics; partitions that never get rewritten after late data.

Incident guidance.

  • Offline queues flush twice: the save_id key makes the second copy a no-op at creation. Analytics deduplicates on save_id too, so counts do not move. Watch the deduplication hit rate spike and confirm that daily totals did not.
  • Session tokens in URLs for two days: stop the extension version or strip at ingestion; re-normalise and overwrite the affected partitions, purge raw copies anywhere downstream, verify, and add a test with known token parameters to the normaliser.
  • Deletes before creates bring pins back: the tombstone was missing or expired too soon. Extend tombstone life to the offline window, reprocess the affected save_ids from the event log, and add a monitor for creates arriving after a tombstone.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Many pins share one save_id: creation returns the first pin for all of them, so saves are lost. Detect a burst of identical ids per client version; repair by replaying the client's queued payloads with a derived id (save_id plus the payload hash) for that version only. (2) Keep a per-domain rule set in the normaliser and re-run it on history with a new version; creators see their pages merged from the version date. (3) Rewrite the partition for the save date; publish a corrected report with a version and a note of how much changed; mark days within the offline window as provisional. (4) Keep the deduplication store keyed by save_id with a TTL of the offline window plus margin; partition it by save_id hash; beyond the window, rely on the unique constraint in the pin store.

Rubric anchors. 2: deduplication by content or time; order by arrival; raw URLs kept. 3: client-minted save id, versioned records with tombstones, URL normalisation, late data rewriting partitions, deletion propagated. 4: also a reasoned save-time rule with both clocks, re-normalisation of history, bounded deduplication with a fallback, and aggregate-only creator views.

Strong signals. Asks how long a phone can stay offline before choosing the deduplication window; treats URL parameters as a privacy question. Red flags. "Deduplicate by image hash"; "the latest event wins" by arrival time.

PIN-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Transactional entities.
    • pins (pin_id, root_pin_id, parent_pin_id NULL, owner_id, board_id NULL, section_id NULL, title, description, created_at, deleted_at NULL). An original has root_pin_id = pin_id and no parent. A copy stores both the root (copied from its parent's root when it is created, so credit is one lookup at any depth) and the parent it was saved from (provenance). Link and image live on the root; a copy carries only its editable text.
    • pin_text_versions (pin_id, version, title, description, edited_at) if edits must be auditable; otherwise the copy row holds the current text.
    • boards (board_id, owner_id, kind personal|group, created_at, deleted_at NULL), sections (section_id, board_id, name, deleted_at NULL), board_collaborators (board_id, pinner_id, role, added_at, removed_at NULL).
    • board_visibility_history (board_id, visibility public|secret, valid_from, valid_to NULL): one row per period, never overwritten.
  • Events (append-only, deduplicated). save_events (save_id, pinner_id, root_pin_id, new_pin_id, parent_pin_id, board_id, section_id, surface, saved_at, board_visibility_at_save) with a uniqueness rule on (pinner_id, board_id, root_pin_id) for live copies so a retried or repeated save to the same board is not a new save; pin_moves (pin_id, from_board, to_board, from_section, to_section, moved_at); pin_deletions (pin_id, deleted_at, reason); board_deletions.
  • The visibility rule (one acceptable choice). A save is judged by the board's visibility at the moment of the save, stamped on the event. A save made while the board was secret never counts, even after the board turns public; saves made after it turns public count from then on. Moving a copy from a secret board to a public board is not a save, so it does not start counting (state the choice; the alternative "counts from the move" is acceptable if written down and consistent).
  • Definition of a save (shared). A save event of a live copy (not deleted, board not deleted, original not deleted as of the computation), on a board that was public at the time of the save. The public count of an original = number of such saves of copies with that root; the creator dashboard = the same events grouped by root and day.
  • Facts.
    • fct_save (one row per save event, with root, creator of the root, saver, board visibility at save, surface, day). Deletions are applied by a deletion job that writes a removed_at and excludes the row from facts within {{deletion_days}} days.
    • agg_creator_root_day (creator_id, root_pin_id, day, saves, saves_removed): rebuilt per day partition from fct_save; past days change only through deletions, recorded as a documented adjustment.
    • pin_public_save_count (root_pin_id, count, as_of): derived from fct_save with a periodic exact recount; an incremental counter is allowed as a cache, never as the source.
    • Unique savers, if offered, are computed per stated window (a week, a month) from the events, or approximated with a sketch per day and merged; they never add up across days.
  • Access. The creator sees aggregates for their own originals; an intermediate saver sees aggregates of saves made from their boards; no one sees who saved to a secret board.

Competing designs to accept. Only parent_pin_id plus a closure or materialised root column maintained by the save service (equivalent). A graph store for provenance with the root denormalised for analytics. Judging visibility by the current board state with a full recompute on every visibility change, if they show the cost and that secret-era saves still never appear (this usually requires the stamp anyway). A separate saves table keyed by (pinner, board, root) with the copy pin created lazily.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Walking parent chains at query time (unbounded depth, broken by deleted intermediates); counters as the source of truth (drift, double counts on retries); joining saves to the board's current visibility (secret saves leaking after a flip); moves counted as saves; deleting rows outright so a creator's past totals change silently; at {{daily_saves}} saves a day, recounting the public count from scratch for every pin.

Incident guidance.

  • Secret saves appeared in creator totals after a board flip: the job joined to current visibility. Contain by recomputing the affected days from events with the visibility stamped at save time (or from board_visibility_history as of saved_at); purge the leaked numbers from caches and exports; add a check that the count of saves with secret-at-save visibility in any public fact is 0.
  • Credit lost at a deleted intermediate copy: the backfill walked parent links. Use the root stored on each copy (stamped at creation, never derived by walking), keep deleted copies as tombstones so lineage stays resolvable, recompute the day, and add a check that every save's root is an original (root_pin_id = pin_id on the root row).
  • Retry doubled save counts: saves were not idempotent. Deduplicate by the uniqueness rule (pinner, board, root) and the client's request id, rebuild the affected counts from events, and add a monitor on saves per (pinner, board, root) > 1.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A is the original (its own root); P's copy root A, parent A, board B1 public: counts; Q's copy root A, parent P's copy, board B2 secret: excluded; the move to B3 is a pin_moves row and, under the stated rule, still excluded. The creator sees 1 save; P sees 1 save made from their board only if Q's save counts under the rule (it does not). (2) Root stamped at creation in O(1) from the parent; a consistency job verifies root rows are originals. (3) The deletion job marks the original's facts removed within {{deletion_days}} days; past daily totals drop with a documented deletion adjustment; copies remain on boards. (4) The collaborator's saves are deleted copies: they leave counts; the collaborator's own history of what they saved stays visible to them until they delete it, if the product says so. (5) One event stream, two aggregations; at {{daily_saves}} a day the public count is incremental with a periodic recount per root.

Rubric anchors. 2: one pins table with a repin counter and no root, visibility as a current flag, deletes as row deletes. 3: root and parent on copies, append-only save events, visibility history with a stated rule, moves not counted, a shared save definition, facts at stated grains. 4: also idempotency on (pinner, board, root), deletion propagation within the window with documented adjustments, intermediate-saver provenance, unique savers handled correctly, and incident guardrails.

Strong signals. States which visibility judges a save before drawing tables; separates credit (root) from provenance (parent). Red flags. Walking the chain for every report; secret saves "filtered later in the dashboard"; counters treated as truth.

PIN-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Content.
    • idea_pins (pin_id, creator_id, created_at, deleted_at NULL).
    • pin_versions (pin_id, version_no, published_at, superseded_at NULL, title, ingredients_or_materials JSON, change_summary): immutable once published; exactly one live version at a time (superseded_at of the previous = published_at of the next).
    • pages (page_id, pin_id, created_in_version): a stable identity; a page keeps its id when its media or text changes.
    • version_pages (pin_id, version_no, page_id, position, media_asset_id, overlay_text): the page's content and its position in that version. A reorder is a new version with new positions; page history follows page_id.
    • media_assets (asset_id, kind image|video, status uploaded|processing|ready|failed, duration_ms NULL, created_at, ready_at NULL); a version can be published only if every version_pages.media_asset_id is ready (checked in the publish transaction).
    • pin_tags (pin_id, version_no, tag_id) for topic tags; page_tags (pin_id, version_no, page_id, kind creator|product, target_id) for creator and product tags.
  • Engagement events. idea_page_views (event_id, session_id, pin_id, version_no, page_id, position, viewed_at, visible_ms), idea_pin_actions (event_id, session_id, pin_id, version_no, page_id NULL, action save|outbound_click|product_tag_click, at). The client sends what it rendered: version, page id and position. Events are deduplicated by event_id; late events keep their version.
  • Definitions. Page view: a page shown for at least the stated threshold. Last page reached in a session: the highest position viewed (not the last one viewed in time, which can be lower after swiping back). Forward progression at position k for a version: sessions that viewed position k+1 ÷ sessions that viewed position k. Drop-off at k: 1 − that ratio.
  • Facts.
    • fct_page_day (pin_id, version_no, page_id, position, day, views, sessions).
    • fct_version_progression (pin_id, version_no, position, sessions_reaching) built from per-session max position.
    • fct_pin_day (pin_id, day, saves, outbound_clicks, product_tag_clicks).
    • The creator report shows per-page history by page id (across versions) and per-position progression per version, with the version boundaries marked.
  • Retention. Raw page views for a few months; per-page and per-version aggregates for the life of the pin. At {{daily_published}} pins a day with up to {{max_pages}} pages, the raw page-view grain is by far the largest table.

Competing designs to accept. Pages stored as an ordered array in the version row (JSON) if each element carries a stable page_id and events reference it. Content-addressed versions (hash of the page list). Event-sourced edits (page_added, page_moved, media_replaced) with versions as projections. Treating a media replacement as a new page, if stated and the creator report explains it.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Positions as page identity (history moves on reorder); attributing events to the current version (late events misattributed); versions edited in place; publishing before media is ready; "drop-off" defined on the last page viewed in time; per-session reconstruction at query time over huge raw tables.

Incident guidance.

  • Events carried position but not page id after a client release: views were keyed by position, so reordered pins (about {{edited_share}} are edited) mixed histories. Contain by marking affected days in reports; repair using the version_pages mapping (version + position → page_id) since the version was still sent; add a contract test and an ingestion check that rejects page views without page_id.
  • A version went live with a page still processing: the publish path did not check media status. Roll the pin back to the previous version (or hide the page), add the ready-check inside the publish transaction, and exclude the affected version's progression from comparisons. With {{video_share}} video pages, the processing queue needs its own backlog alert.
  • Earlier versions rewritten in place: immutability was not enforced. Restore versions from the change log or backups, make version rows append-only (no UPDATE grant on published versions), and route tag corrections through a new version.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Version 2: positions P3=1, P1=2, P2=3; P2 keeps its page_id with a new media asset; P2's view history continues by page id and the report marks the media change. (2) Events carry version 1, so they are attributed to version 1 and its positions; no inference from the live version. (3) Sessions reaching each position per version; comparing versions compares progression curves, labelled with what changed. (4) The tag on earlier versions stays as history; the live version shows it as unavailable or drops it in a new version; counted clicks remain. (5) Raw per-page events for weeks to months, daily per-page aggregates long term; sessions × average pages viewed gives the raw volume.

Rubric anchors. 2: pin row with a pages array keyed by position and no versions. 3: immutable versions, stable page ids, version_pages with positions, events with version and page, defined progression. 4: also the media-ready publish rule, late-event attribution, per-page versus per-position reporting, retention sizing, and incident guardrails.

Strong signals. Distinguishes page identity from position unprompted; defines the last page reached as the maximum position. Red flags. Joining events to the current version; editing published versions; showing individual viewers to creators.

PIN-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Merchants and uploads. merchants (merchant_id, country, default_currency, created_at), catalogues (catalogue_id, merchant_id, feed_url_ref, schedule), feed_uploads (upload_id, catalogue_id, fetched_at, row_count, status received|validated|applied|rejected, rejection_reason), feed_rows (upload_id, merchant_item_id, item_group_id, title, link, image_url, price_minor, sale_price_minor NULL, sale_start NULL, sale_end NULL, currency, availability): immutable, retained for a limited period (raw files in cheap storage).
  • Product identity. products (product_key, merchant_id, merchant_item_id, first_seen_upload, status active|missing|retired, identity_fingerprint); a unique constraint on (merchant_id, merchant_item_id) among active products. A re-used item id (fingerprint mismatch: different link path and title) retires the old product_key and creates a new one; the old pins stay on the old key and show "no longer available".
  • History. product_attr_history (product_key, valid_from, valid_to NULL, item_group_id, title, link, image_url), price_history (product_key, valid_from, valid_to NULL, price_minor, sale_price_minor NULL, sale_start NULL, sale_end NULL, currency), availability_history (product_key, valid_from, valid_to NULL, availability). Intervals are produced by diffing a validated upload against current state; unchanged items write nothing. Price shown at time t = sale price if sale_start ≤ t < sale_end, else price, from the interval containing t.
  • Product pins. product_pins (pin_id, product_key, created_at); never re-pointed silently; a deliberate re-map is logged in product_pin_remaps.
  • Validation. Before applying: row-count drop versus the previous upload beyond a threshold, share of zero or null prices, share of availability flips, currency changes, duplicate item ids. A failed upload is rejected, the previous state stays live, and the merchant is notified with the reason.
  • Engagement facts. fct_product_engagement_day (merchant_id, product_key, item_group_id_at_event, day, impressions, saves, outbound_clicks) with the item group stamped at event time; a merchant view by current grouping is a separate, labelled re-aggregation. Money-weighted reports convert with fx_rates (currency, day, rate) and fail closed on a missing rate.
  • Sizing. {{catalogue_items}} items refreshed every {{feed_hours}} hours: even a 1–2% change rate per upload is millions of interval rows a day; full snapshots per upload would be orders of magnitude larger.

Competing designs to accept. SCD type 2 on one wide product table (if they limit which attributes create versions). Periodic full snapshots with a compacted change log (if "price on a date" is answered by the log). Feed deltas computed by hashing rows per item and comparing hashes. Storing a per-upload "applied state" pointer and serving from immutable upload data, if the cost is shown.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwritten prices (no history); full copies per upload; floats for money; summing across currencies; deleting missing items (pins and saves orphaned, then resurrected with new ids); re-used ids silently re-pointing pins; applying a bad upload; title changes in every upload exploding SCD versions.

Incident guidance.

  • All prices 0 after an export bug: validation lacked a zero-price share check. Contain by restoring the previous state for that catalogue (re-apply the last good upload), suppress price-drop notices generated in that {{feed_hours}}-hour window, and add a check that rejects an upload whose zero-price share or median price change exceeds a threshold.
  • Re-used item ids after a migration: identity was the merchant item id alone. Detect with a fingerprint (link path, title similarity, image hash); retire old keys, move pins only by explicit merchant mapping, and cancel notices tied to mismatched products; add the fingerprint check to every upload.
  • Missing exchange rate treated as 1: the report defaulted the rate. Make the conversion fail closed (no number rather than a wrong one), backfill the rate, restate the report with a label, and alert on missing rates for any of the {{currencies}} currencies before reports run.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Price interval closes and a new one opens on the drop; availability interval out_of_stock; the weekend sale is stored as sale_price with its window, so no new interval is needed at start and end if the window is in the row; back in stock at full price closes the sale (or it simply ends). (2) Row-count drop check rejects; the previous state stays; the merchant sees a rejected upload with the reason. (3) Fingerprint mismatch → new product key; old pins show unavailable; engagement stays with the old key. (4) Change set ≈ items × change rate per upload × uploads a day; compute by hashing each item's relevant fields and comparing with the stored hash. (5) Use the item group at event time by default, offer the current grouping as a labelled view; convert with the rate of the event day.

Rubric anchors. 2: one products table overwritten by each feed, prices as floats, deletes for missing items. 3: immutable uploads, product state, price/availability intervals, minor units with currency, stable product keys for pins. 4: also validation that blocks bad uploads, re-used id detection, sale-window semantics, item-group history in facts, fail-closed currency conversion and a change-set estimate.

Strong signals. Asks what "price shown" means during a sale; protects pins from identity changes. Red flags. Floats for money; summing currencies; treating a missing item as deleted forever after one upload.

PIN-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Evidence. verification_checks (check_id, claim_id, method meta_tag|dns_record|file, result pass|fail|error, detail, checked_at): append-only, kept for audit. Errors (timeouts, resolver failures) are distinct from fails.
  • Claim state. claims (claim_id, account_id, domain, requested_at); claim_state_history (claim_id, state pending|verified|failing|lost|released, valid_from, valid_to NULL, cause_check_id NULL). Failing starts at the first failed check; lost starts at failing_start + {{grace_hours}} hours if no passing check came first; a passing check during failing returns to verified.
  • Derived intervals. claim_intervals (domain, account_id, claim_id, valid_from, valid_to NULL): the periods in state verified or failing, computed once from the state history (the grace period is applied here, and only here). A constraint (an exclusion constraint on tstzrange per domain, or a check in the writer) prevents overlaps.
  • Hosts. pin_links (pin_id, url, created_at); link_resolutions (url, final_url, resolved_at, crawler_run) for redirects and shorteners; pin_hosts (pin_id, host, rule_version, derived_at), where the rule lower-cases, strips one leading www., removes tracking parameters, and uses the resolved URL when the link is a known redirector. A rule change writes new rows with a new version and triggers recomputation of affected facts.
  • Subdomains. A claim covers the domain and its subdomains (host = domain or host ends with '.' || domain); the most specific claim in force wins.
  • Crediting. At ingestion (or in an hourly batch), each engagement event is joined to the claim interval covering its host at its event time and the credited account is stored on fct_pin_engagement (event_id, pin_id, event_type, event_time, host, credited_account_id NULL, credit_rule_version). Late events are credited by event time against the interval table, which still holds past intervals. Daily agg_creator_day (account_id, day, impressions, saves, outbound_clicks) is built from the fact.
  • Creator view. Shows claim coverage per day (hours with no claim in force) next to the metrics, so a dip from a lost claim is visible.

Competing designs to accept. Computing credit at report time with an as-of join (correct, more expensive; they should say how to keep it cheap — sorted interval lookups per domain, broadcast of the small interval table). Applying the grace period at query time, if it is applied in exactly one place. Storing claims as a type 2 table directly instead of a state history plus intervals.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Credit by pin creation time or by the current claim (history moves with the domain); grace applied twice or not at all; suffix tests without the dot; normalisation drift between ingestion and reports; a resolver outage that turns errors into fails; joining billions of events to claims without partitioning by domain.

Incident guidance.

  • DNS outage makes checks fail longer than the {{grace_hours}}-hour grace period: classify resolver errors as error, not fail, and do not advance claims to lost on errors; pause loss for the affected provider with a recorded decision; re-check when resolution recovers. Guardrail: an alert when the share of failing claims jumps, and a rule that a mass failure from one provider needs a human decision.
  • Job credited by the current claim: history moved to the new owner. Restore from the fact's stored credited account (or recompute with the as-of join), notify both creators, and add a test with a mid-period transfer that the previous owner's past numbers do not change.
  • Normalisation stopped stripping www.: affected pins were credited to nobody. Re-derive hosts with the fixed rule for the affected window, recompute facts for those pins, label the restatement, and add a monitor on the share of linked-pin events credited to nobody (claim checks every {{recheck_days}} days cannot see this).

Follow-up guidance. (1) With 24 hours of grace: failing from day 3 10:00, lost at day 4 10:00, verified again at day 5 09:00 (a new interval); with 72 hours the pass at day 5 09:00 lands inside the grace period and the claim was never lost. Released a week later ends the interval; the next account's interval starts at its own verification. (2) Coverage hours per day next to metrics. (3) The late event is credited by its event time to the previous owner. (4) Re-derive hosts, recompute the affected facts, show a restatement note. (5) Partition events by host or domain, broadcast the small interval table, or stamp credit at ingestion.

Rubric anchors. 2: a claims table with a status column and credit by joining pins to today's claims. 3: evidence, state history and intervals; credit by event time; stated normalisation and subdomain rules. 4: also grace applied once with exact boundaries, errors versus fails, versioned host rules with restatement, credit stored on the fact, coverage shown to creators, and incident guardrails.

Strong signals. Separates evidence from state from intervals; tests the suffix rule with a look-alike host. Red flags. Credit by pin creator; re-crediting history when a domain changes hands; ignoring redirects entirely.

PIN-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH ev AS (                                   -- countable events on pins with a link, host normalised
  SELECT e.event_id, e.event_type, e.occurred_at,
         regexp_replace(lower(p.link_host), '^www\.', '') AS host
  FROM pin_events e
  JOIN pins p ON p.pin_id = e.pin_id
  WHERE e.event_type IN ('impression', 'save', 'outbound_click')
    AND p.link_host IS NOT NULL
), credited AS (                               -- one claim per event: the most specific in force
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (ev.event_id)
         ev.event_id, ev.event_type, ev.occurred_at, c.creator_id
  FROM ev
  JOIN domain_claims c
    ON (ev.host = c.domain OR right(ev.host, length(c.domain) + 1) = '.' || c.domain)
   AND c.claimed_at <= ev.occurred_at
   AND (c.released_at IS NULL OR ev.occurred_at < c.released_at)
  ORDER BY ev.event_id, length(c.domain) DESC
)
SELECT creator_id,
       date_trunc('week', occurred_at)::date AS week_start,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'impression')     AS impressions,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'save')           AS saves,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'outbound_click') AS outbound_clicks
FROM credited
GROUP BY creator_id, week_start
ORDER BY creator_id, week_start;

Explanation. Credit is a property of each event, so the join to claims is an as-of join on the event's occurred_at with a half-open interval: in force from claimed_at inclusive to released_at exclusive, which makes a transfer at one instant credit exactly one creator. Filtering the event types before the join removes closeups, so no creator-week row exists with all counts 0, and the inner join drops events nobody is credited for. The host is normalised once (lower case, one leading www. removed); at Medium the hosts are already normalised, so it changes nothing there. At Very Hard a host can be covered by a claim on its parent domain and by a claim on the subdomain itself; DISTINCT ON (event_id) … ORDER BY length(domain) DESC keeps only the most specific claim, so the event is counted once. The suffix test is anchored on a dot (right(host, len + 1) = '.' || domain), so a look-alike host that merely ends with the claimed name is not covered. At Medium and Hard the data contains no subdomain hosts, so the subdomain clause is harmless there and a candidate's exact-match query is equally correct. date_trunc('week', …) returns the Monday in the session time zone, which the setup sets to UTC.

Complexity. One hash join of events to pins, then a join to claims on the host. The equality part hashes; the suffix part is a nested loop over claims per event in this form, which is fine for a sample and not at scale. In production, derive each event's candidate domains (the host and each parent suffix: a.b.c.example → a.b.c.example, b.c.example, c.example) and equi-join on them, or stamp the credited creator at ingestion. The claims table is small enough to broadcast.

Dialect notes. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL; Snowflake and BigQuery use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY LENGTH(domain) DESC) = 1, Spark SQL and MySQL 8 a subquery on that row number. COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) becomes COUNT_IF(…) in Snowflake and Spark, COUNTIF(…) in BigQuery and SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) in MySQL. Week starts: DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', ts) starts on Monday in Snowflake by default (WEEK_START parameter), BigQuery needs DATE_TRUNC(DATE(ts), WEEK(MONDAY)) because plain WEEK starts on Sunday, Spark's date_trunc('week', ts) starts on Monday, and MySQL needs DATE(ts) - INTERVAL WEEKDAY(ts) DAY. regexp_replace exists in all of them; MySQL's RIGHT and LENGTH behave the same for ASCII hosts (use CHAR_LENGTH for non-ASCII). None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. An event exactly at a claim's claimed_at (credited); a domain transferred to another creator at one instant with an event exactly at that instant (the new owner only); a pin created before its domain was claimed, with events before (nobody) and after (the creator) the claim; a transferred domain's older pin with events on both sides of the transfer; events at Sunday 23:59:59 and Monday 00:00:00 UTC on either side of a week boundary; a creator claimed late in the last week whose events after the claim are all closeups (no row); pins with no link and a pin on a domain nobody claims. Hard adds hosts with capitals and a leading www. (forced on credited pins), a claim that lapses and is re-verified by the same creator after a gap (events in the gap credit nobody; an event exactly at the re-verification is credited) and, in some seeds, a claim released for good. Very Hard adds a subdomain claimed by another creator for part of the period (the subdomain's creator wins while both are in force, the parent's before), an unclaimed subdomain (the parent's creator), and a look-alike host such as the + the claimed domain (nobody).

Common mistakes. Crediting by the claim in force when the pin was created; crediting by the latest claim; an inclusive released_at (double credit at a transfer) or an exclusive claimed_at; Sunday-start weeks; counting closeups or grouping before filtering the types (zero rows); a LEFT JOIN that keeps uncredited events as NULL-creator rows; (Hard+) comparing raw hosts; (Very Hard) exact matching only, crediting both the parent and the subdomain claims, letting the parent win, or a suffix test without the dot. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Generate candidate suffixes per host and equi-join, partition by domain, broadcast claims; or stamp at ingestion. (2) Stamping at ingestion fixes history and makes reports cheap, but late events must still be credited by event time against interval history, and a host-rule change needs a recomputation; computing at report time is always consistent with the current intervals but costs a join every time. (3) Per creator and week, sum the overlap of the gaps between their claim intervals with the week (tstzrange intersection, or LEAST/GREATEST arithmetic). (4) Apply the grace period once, when claim intervals are derived, so released_at already includes it; this query should not add it again.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but credits by pin creation or the latest claim, or counts closeups. 3: matches the expected result at the level played. 4: also explains how to scale the as-of join, where to store the credited creator, and how to report coverage gaps.

Strong signals. Writes the half-open interval without being asked; asks what happens at the instant of a transfer; anchors the suffix on a dot. Red flags. Joining pins to domain_claims WHERE released_at IS NULL; LIKE '%' || domain; a GROUP BY over all event types with zero-count rows left in.
PIN-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH ev AS (                                   -- countable events on pins with a link, host normalised
  SELECT e.event_id, e.event_type, e.occurred_at,
         regexp_replace(lower(p.link_host), '^www\.', '') AS host
  FROM pin_events e
  JOIN pins p ON p.pin_id = e.pin_id
  WHERE e.event_type IN ('impression', 'save', 'outbound_click')
    AND p.link_host IS NOT NULL
), credited AS (                               -- one claim per event: the most specific in force
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (ev.event_id)
         ev.event_id, ev.event_type, ev.occurred_at, c.creator_id
  FROM ev
  JOIN domain_claims c
    ON (ev.host = c.domain OR right(ev.host, length(c.domain) + 1) = '.' || c.domain)
   AND c.claimed_at <= ev.occurred_at
   AND (c.released_at IS NULL OR ev.occurred_at < c.released_at)
  ORDER BY ev.event_id, length(c.domain) DESC
)
SELECT creator_id,
       date_trunc('week', occurred_at)::date AS week_start,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'impression')     AS impressions,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'save')           AS saves,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'outbound_click') AS outbound_clicks
FROM credited
GROUP BY creator_id, week_start
ORDER BY creator_id, week_start;

PIN-L4-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Grid and slot ids: the server issues a grid_view_id with each feed, search, related or board response and records the pins it returned in which slots (a served log). The client tracks each tile with (grid_view_id, slot_id, pin_id); slot ids are stable for the life of the grid, independent of on-screen position, so a reflow or rotation does not create a new identity.
  • Client rule (versioned): the rendering layer computes, per tile, the fraction of the tile inside the visible viewport (not the laid-out area) and a dwell timer; when it holds ≥ {{visible_pct}}% for ≥ {{dwell_ms}} ms, it emits one impression with impression_id (a UUID or hash(grid_view_id, slot_id, visit_no)), rule_version, client_version, client timestamp and a monotonic sequence number. The client also applies the {{revisit_minutes}}-minute rule locally per grid view (cheap and it saves bandwidth), and the server re-applies it authoritatively.
  • Batching and upload: impressions are written to a small on-disk queue (not only memory), flushed every few seconds or on backgrounding, retried with backoff, and capped in size; the server returns per-batch acknowledgements. No network call per impression.
  • Ingestion: an HTTP collector stamps server_received_at and writes to a durable log partitioned by grid_view_id (so one grid's events meet in one place). A stream job deduplicates by impression_id, joins to the served log to validate (the pin was actually served in that grid; unknown grid ids or impossible sequences are invalid), applies the scroll-back rule by (grid_view_id, pin_id) within {{revisit_minutes}} minutes, and drops invalid traffic.
  • Time and late data: estimate each device's clock offset per batch (server_received_at − client send time, using the batch header) and correct event times; events whose corrected time is implausible use receive time. A day's creator aggregates are updated as late events arrive; the billing day closes at +48 hours, and later events are recorded as adjustments to a later invoice rather than edits to the closed day.
  • Aggregates: per (pin, surface, day) impressions, with closeups and saves alongside, for creator analytics (fast path, hours behind); a separate billing pipeline over the same deduplicated events, with reconciliation counts (events received, deduped, invalid, billed) per day and per client version. Reports show counts only.
  • Consistency across clients: scripted scroll sessions run on each client in CI against a fake server (golden counts); in production, monitor impressions per closeup, per save and per served pin by client and version; new client versions roll out with a canary and a gate on those ratios.
  • Scale: {{daily_impressions}} a day is hundreds of thousands to millions of events a second at peak; at ~100 bytes compressed per event, tens of TB per day of raw events, which the billing audit period multiplies; per-pin daily rows are far smaller (one row per pin shown that day).

Competing designs to accept. Server-side deduplication only (client sends every visibility episode) if they account for bandwidth. Using the served log as the denominator and client events as confirmations. A lambda-style split or a single streaming pipeline with a closed batch recompute for billing. Exact dedup by key in a state store versus a daily batch dedup for billing.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Rule drift between clients; pre-rendering counted as visible; in-memory buffers lost on background kill; clock skew moving events between days; position-based keys double counting after reflows; retries duplicating batches; a closed billing day that keeps changing.

Incident guidance.

  • +35% on one app after pre-rendering: correlate by client version; ratios of impressions to closeups and saves broke. Hotfix the client to measure the visible viewport; exclude or correct the affected version's impressions in billing with a recorded adjustment (served log plus corrected rule), and annotate creator analytics. Prevention: golden scroll tests and canary gates on ratios.
  • −12% from background kills: the version's events are lost, not late. Ship a persistent queue and flush on backgrounding; be honest that lost impressions cannot be recovered for billing (under-billing is the advertiser-friendly error), and note the gap for creators. Prevention: per-version volume monitors relative to sessions.
  • Rotation double counts within {{revisit_minutes}} minutes: the dedup key used position. Re-key on (grid_view_id, pin_id) with stable slot ids, recompute affected days from raw events before billing closes, and adjust closed days. Prevention: keys reviewed as part of the rule version; a test that rotates mid-scroll.
  • Clocks a day ahead: day assignment must not trust the device; correct with the batch offset and fall back to receive time; move misplaced events into the right day (or into an adjustment if that day is closed). Prevention: monitor the share of events whose corrected time differs from receive time by more than an hour.

Follow-up guidance. Make them trace the scroll-back case precisely and say where each rule runs; push on the billing close and adjustments; ask for the numbers.

Rubric anchors. 2: "log an impression when the pin renders", one pipeline, client timestamps trusted, no dedup key. 3: client visibility rule with grid and slot ids, idempotent batching, server dedup and validation against the served log, late-data policy, separate creator and billing aggregates. 4: also versioned rules with cross-client golden tests and canary gates, clock-offset correction, closed-day adjustments, invalid-traffic filtering, volume and cost estimates, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks what "seen" means before designing; distinguishes laid-out from visible; joins impressions to what the server actually served. Red flags. Counting renders; per-impression network calls; editing closed billing days; reports that list who saw a pin.

PIN-L4-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Catalogue ingestion: each upload is parsed and validated (schema, currency, price ranges, image fetchability), then diffed against the merchant's last accepted catalogue by product id: added, removed, changed (price, availability, title, image). Guard rails quarantine suspicious uploads: more than a set share of products flipping to out of stock or removed, or mass id churn (many removals matched by many additions with the same titles and images). A quarantined upload alerts the merchant and keeps the last good catalogue, within the freshness constraint (if no good upload arrives within {{refresh_hours}} hours, prices are hidden rather than shown stale).
  • Offers store: current price, currency and availability per (merchant, product), keyed for fast lookup, updated from accepted diffs, with as_of = upload time. The products panel resolves price and stock here at serving time, so price and stock freshness do not depend on re-matching. Removals propagate from the diff to the offers store within minutes, which meets the one-hour rule.
  • Embedding index: product image embeddings per (product, image hash, model version); only added or changed images are embedded. An approximate nearest-neighbour index per category (or partitioned by category) supports incremental inserts and deletes, with periodic compaction. Each index is tagged with the embedding model version.
  • Detections and links: pins are processed in priority order (by recent impressions); the given detector produces boxes and categories once per image (cached by image hash and detector version). For each detection, query vectors are compared against the same-version index; the given scoring function orders candidates. A link row stores (pin_id, detection_id, candidate product ids, scores, detector_version, embedding_version, index_snapshot, created_at); merchant-tagged exact links are stored separately with higher trust.
  • Refresh: when products are removed or go out of stock, affected links are found through an inverted index (product → links) and their candidate lists refilled from the index, lazily on read for long-tail pins and eagerly for popular pins. New products are matched into popular pins' detections by a periodic job, bounded by budget.
  • Model migration: build the new-version index in full alongside the old (dual index), re-embed products and pins' detections, switch query and index together per category behind a flag after offline and online checks (outbound clicks per panel open, coverage), then retire the old index.
  • Click measurement: outbound clicks go through a redirect that records (click_id, pin_id, detection_id, product_id, merchant_id, link versions, served_at); dedup by click id, filter invalid traffic (rate limits per network and device, known bots, impossible sequences), aggregate per merchant, product, link version and day; promoted product pin billing reads the same filtered events, so merchant reports and bills agree. Merchants see aggregates only.
  • Evaluation of matching: holdouts or interleaving between matching versions, measuring outbound clicks and saves per panel open; credit a version only for clicks on links it produced.

Competing designs to accept. On-demand matching at tap time with a fast vector index if they show the 300 ms budget holds and cache results. A single global index instead of per-category ones. Batch-only refresh if they still meet the one-hour removal rule through serving-time checks against the offers store.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Full rebuilds that cannot keep up with uploads; mismatched embedding versions between query and index; trusting a broken upload; product id churn orphaning links; stale caches showing old prices; bot clicks inflating merchant reports and bills.

Incident guidance.

  • Whole catalogue marked out of stock: should have been quarantined as a mass change. Restore the last good catalogue's availability, notify the merchant, and add the mass-change guard. If already applied, the offers store can be rolled back from the previous accepted version. Prevention: thresholds on per-upload change rates, with merchant confirmation for large changes.
  • Query-side model rolled ahead of the index: comparing vectors from different spaces; roll the query side back immediately, then migrate with a dual index switched per category together. Prevention: version tags checked at query time (refuse cross-version comparisons) and an online guard on outbound clicks per panel open.
  • Product id change: detect id churn by matching removed and added products on stable attributes (GTIN where present, image hash, title, link); map old ids to new ids and re-point links; contact the merchant. Prevention: id-churn detection in the diff and a quarantine.
  • Tenfold clicks from a few networks: invalid traffic; filter it from merchant reports and bills (credit if already billed) and keep the raw record for audit. Prevention: real-time invalid-traffic rules and anomaly alerts per merchant.

Follow-up guidance. Push on the rate-of-change separation, how a removal reaches every link within the hour, and the dual-index migration; ask for the daily re-match cost at {{merchants}} merchants and {{refresh_hours}}-hour refreshes.

Rubric anchors. 2: rebuild everything nightly, prices stored inside links, no versioning, clicks counted raw. 3: validated catalogue diffs, an offers store resolved at serving time, incremental index updates, versioned links, deduplicated and filtered click measurement. 4: also quarantine for suspicious uploads, a safe embedding migration, product-to-link inverted index for targeted refresh, honest matching evaluation, merchant reports consistent with billing, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks how often each piece changes before choosing stores; treats the merchant's upload as untrusted input. Red flags. Showing stale prices to avoid empty panels; comparing vectors from different model versions; reports that expose pinners.

PIN-L4-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Model: pin(pin_id, creator_id, original_pin_id, media, created_at), board(board_id, owner_id, visibility, is_group, created_at), section(section_id, board_id, rank), board_member(board_id, pinner_id, role, added_at, removed_at), save(save_id, board_id, section_id, pin_id, saver_id, rank_key, saved_at, deleted_at), follow(follower_id, target_type, target_id, followed_at).
  • Source of truth and derived copies: saves are stored partitioned by board_id (board pages are the dominant read and a board's pins live together); a derived index by (saver_id, pin_id) answers "already saved by me", and one by pin_id feeds public save counts. Derived copies are built from the save store's change stream (CDC or an outbox), which also carries visibility with every event. The saver's own board view reads the primary, so their write is visible at once.
  • Ordering: each save has a rank_key (lexicographic, fractional indexing); newest-first boards assign keys that sort before the current first; a drag writes one new key between its neighbours. Keys grow when pins are repeatedly inserted between the same neighbours; a background job rebalances a board's keys (rewriting them evenly) when the longest key passes a length limit, with a board version so concurrent readers page consistently. Concurrent drags: last writer wins per pin, with a board version returned to clients so they refresh; a new save never conflicts with a reorder because it only takes a new key.
  • Counters: public save count per pin and follower count per board or profile are aggregated from the derived streams in short windows (sharded counters or a stream aggregation with periodic flush), so a viral pin is one batched update a second, not thousands of row increments. Only events whose visibility is public contribute; a visibility change emits compensating events (subtract the board's saves from public counts when it turns secret, add them back when public).
  • Public surfaces from a public-only projection: board pages for non-owners, profiles, search and related pins consume a projection containing only saves on public boards. When a board turns secret, one visibility event drives: removal from the projection, purge of cached board and profile pages (CDN purge by surrogate key such as board:<id>), deletion from the search and related-pins candidate stores, and compensating counter updates, all within {{visibility_minutes}} minutes, with a tracker that confirms each consumer has applied the change.
  • Permissions: group board membership read from an authoritative store with short-lived caches invalidated by membership events; writes check membership at the server.
  • Scale: {{saves}} saves at ~100 bytes is tens of TB before replicas and indexes; {{peak_saves}} saves a second are spread across board partitions; the hot spots are counters and viral pins, not boards.
  • Leak check: a continuous job samples public surfaces (search results, cached board pages, related candidates) and checks every pin-board pair against current visibility, alerting on any secret pair.

Competing designs to accept. Partitioning by owner with boards co-located (good for profiles, worse for group boards); integer positions with gaps instead of string ranks if they handle renumbering; strongly consistent counters for small boards and aggregated ones only for hot items. Filtering visibility at read time in addition to a projection, as defence in depth.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Hot counters on viral pins and popular boards; cache copies that outlive a visibility change; long rank keys; stale permission caches; consumers that miss a visibility event; counters that go down and up visibly.

Incident guidance.

  • Secret board still public after 40 minutes: caches and the search index were not tied to the visibility event. Purge by surrogate key now, force a reindex of the board's pins, and confirm with the leak check. Prevention: one visibility event fanned out to every consumer with acknowledgements and a deadline alarm at {{visibility_minutes}} minutes.
  • Viral pin at 8,000 saves a second: per-save increments on one row; stop synchronous counter writes, move to windowed aggregation or sharded counters, and drain retries with backoff. Prevention: counters off the save path by design.
  • Rank keys of hundreds of characters: rebalance affected boards in the background with board versioning; add a key-length trigger. Prevention: rebalancing as routine, not as a repair.
  • Removed collaborator saving for 30 minutes: the app's permission cache refreshed only at login. Enforce membership at the server on every write, invalidate caches on membership events, and audit saves made in the window (remove them if the owner wishes). Prevention: authorisation never decided by a client cache.

Follow-up guidance. Have them list every public surface for the secret-board question; push on the hot counter with numbers; make them write the rank keys for a drag between two pins.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table, ORDER BY position with renumbering, counts by COUNT(*), visibility checked only on the board page. 3: board-partitioned saves with derived indexes, rank keys, aggregated counters excluding secret saves, visibility propagated through change events to public surfaces. 4: also rank-key rebalancing with a concurrency rule, compensating counter events, cache purge by surrogate key with acknowledgement tracking, server-side permission checks, a continuous leak check, numbers, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Enumerates the public surfaces before designing; treats visibility as data in the stream. Red flags. Filtering secret saves only in the UI; counters updated synchronously per save; renumbering a whole board on every drag.

PIN-L4-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Inputs: search events (normalised term: case-folded, punctuation and whitespace normalised, light stemming or a lemma, spelling variants mapped through a maintained dictionary; terms matching the exclusion lists dropped here) and save events mapped to topics through the given taxonomy. Region from coarse location at event time. Raw query text exists only inside the aggregation job and in a short-retention raw store.
  • Weekly aggregation: per (term or topic, region, week), distinct pinners. Exact distinct counts (a set of pseudonymous pinner ids per cell within the job) for cells near the threshold; mergeable sketches (HyperLogLog) for large cells and for rollups across regions or weeks, which merge without double counting. Retain weekly cells (counts plus sketches for the allowed rollups) for {{years}} years; raw events for a short period only.
  • Thresholds and differencing: a cell is shown only if distinct pinners ≥ {{min_pinners}}, decided on the exact count near the boundary. Users choose from fixed region and topic groupings; when a parent is shown and some children are suppressed, suppress enough siblings (or the complement) that no suppressed cell can be derived by subtraction. One threshold service is used by every consumer, so no other dashboard shows unsuppressed cells.
  • Normalised interest: the interest index is distinct searching (or saving) pinners per million active pinners in that region and week, then scaled 0–100 over the displayed period, stated in the tool. Dividing by active pinners removes growth of the user base; per-series scaling makes small and large regions comparable in shape.
  • Week alignment: weeks are Monday-start ISO weeks in each region's local time; year over year compares each week with the week exactly 364 days earlier, which keeps weekdays aligned and gives week 53 a defined comparison (whatever that earlier week's number is); the rule is stated in the tool. Known moving holidays are labelled on the chart, and the rising list uses a 364-day comparison plus a multi-week baseline.
  • Rising terms: growth of the smoothed index this week versus the baseline (for example the last eight weeks and the same weeks last year), with a minimum volume floor well above the threshold and shrinkage of small counts (for example a lower confidence bound on the ratio), so 3 → 30 does not top the list.
  • Invalid traffic: before aggregation, drop automated clients and cap contributions per pinner per term per week (one pinner counts once anyway); anomaly checks on searches per pinner per term flag farms.
  • Serving: precompute the weekly cells and the common rollups into a columnar store or OLAP cube; queries over fixed groupings answer in well under 2 seconds. The rising list is computed once per week.
  • Scale: {{terms}} terms × {{regions}} regions × 52 × {{years}} cells is the theoretical upper bound; most cells are empty or suppressed, so storage is dominated by the non-empty cells (store sparse).

Competing designs to accept. Differential privacy noise instead of (or in addition to) thresholds, if they explain the accuracy cost for small regions. Topic-only reporting with no free terms. Calendar-month reporting if they argue it for planning users, with the same alignment care.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Counting events instead of pinners; differencing across overlapping groupings; week misalignment; taxonomy changes breaking series; raw query text leaking into downstream tables; inconsistent suppression across tools.

Incident guidance.

  • Everything +15% in January: week 1 compared with a week covering different holidays and days. Switch to a 364-day comparison or explicit alignment, recompute the affected weeks, and annotate the chart. Prevention: a calendar table with ISO weeks, 53-week years and holiday flags used by every comparison, with a test for the year boundary.
  • Bot-driven rising term: counts were of searches. Recompute with distinct pinners and invalid-traffic filtering, pull the term from the rising list, and explain the correction to users. Prevention: per-pinner caps, anomaly checks on searches per pinner, and the rising list built only from distinct-pinner cells.
  • Flickering cells and an unsuppressed second dashboard: flicker near the threshold is expected; consider smoothing over several weeks or showing a "not enough data" marker instead of a gap. The second dashboard is a privacy incident: take it down, move it onto the shared threshold service, and review who accessed it. Prevention: one suppression service; no direct access to unsuppressed cells.
  • Taxonomy split: series for new topics start from zero. Re-map history: re-classify the historical saves (if raw data still exists) or apportion the old topic's history by the post-split mix with a clear "estimated" label; keep the old topic's series available for comparison. Prevention: taxonomy versions with explicit mappings applied to history.

Follow-up guidance. Make them show a concrete differencing attack and its fix; push on the meaning of the number shown and on week 53.

Rubric anchors. 2: counts of searches per term and week, a threshold per cell, year over year by calendar week number. 3: distinct pinners, thresholds with fixed groupings, a normalised index with a stated meaning, a week rule that handles 53-week years, invalid-traffic filtering, a precomputed serving layer. 4: also complement suppression with one shared suppression service, exact counts near the threshold with sketches elsewhere, a robust rising measure with baselines and floors, taxonomy versioning with history mapping, raw text confinement, numbers, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks what the number means to a planner before designing; raises differencing unprompted. Red flags. Breakdowns by inferred personal attributes; raw query text in long-lived tables; ranking terms by percent growth from tiny bases.

PIN-L4-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Events: each stage emits (pin_id, stage, attempt, status: started|finished|failed|queued_for_review, service_ts, emitted_seq) asynchronously to a durable log; the upload service emits created with the server's receive time. The collector adds ingest_ts. Events carry no media.
  • Lifecycle table: one row per pin, folded from events by a stream job: first created, first successful finished per stage (idempotent: a replayed or duplicate event cannot move a timestamp backwards or forwards once set, except by an explicit retry attempt), current stage, deletion time, segments (media type, size, creator size band, region, client). Eligibility is "all required stages finished"; first impression comes from the serving log as a separate field.
  • One timeline: stage durations computed within the same clock where possible (each service reports queued_at and finished_at from its own clock, so the work time is clock-consistent), and cross-service waits from ordered ingest times; services' clock offsets estimated from paired events and alarmed; negative durations are counted and surfaced as a data-quality metric, never silently clipped.
  • Reporting: hourly cohorts by upload hour: share eligible within {{target_minutes}} minutes, survival curves (Kaplan–Meier style, with unfinished pins censored at the current time and deleted pins censored at deletion), percentiles once a cohort is complete, and the stage breakdown (queue wait versus work time per stage). Segment by media type, creator size, region and review status; alert on any segment breaching target, not just the total.
  • Separate eligibility from distribution: "time to eligibility" is the pipeline's goal; "time from eligibility to first impression" depends on demand and the given scoring function and is reported separately so pipeline work is not judged by it.
  • Pipeline changes: from the queue-versus-work breakdown: per-creator fair queuing (a creator's bulk upload is processed in parallel but cannot take more than a share of a queue), priority lanes, autoscaling on queue age (not queue length), smaller batches in feature extraction so a pin is not held for a whole batch, and review staffing or automatic triage measured against the review segment. Prove impact with before-and-after survival curves per segment.
  • Creator view: a creator sees their own pins' status (processing, in review, live) without stage internals.

Competing designs to accept. Distributed tracing with a trace per pin instead of a custom event stream (accept if they handle replays and long waits beyond typical trace retention). A batch hourly fold instead of streaming. Reporting medians plus "share stuck beyond N hours" instead of survival curves, if stuck pins are clearly counted.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Clock skew between services; batch-stamped timestamps; replays double counting; survivorship bias in medians; a single creator's burst starving others; overall percentiles hiding segments.

Incident guidance.

  • Video p95 at four hours, overall near target: the segment alert should fire; the transcoding queue is dominated by one creator's batch. Apply per-creator fair queuing, scale transcoding on queue age, and process the batch in parallel at a capped share. Prevention: per-segment alerting and fairness by design.
  • Negative durations after a deploy: the service stamps batches, not pins. Roll back or fix to stamp each pin's finish; recompute affected rows from ingest times; keep the negative-duration metric as an alarm. Prevention: contract tests on stage events (finish after start for the same service).
  • Weekend review backlog and an improving median: the median excludes unfinished pins. Switch the headline to share within target with censored pins counted; staff or triage the review queue. Prevention: survival-based reporting and an alert on queue age for review.
  • Indexing replay, pins eligible twice: the fold must ignore a second finished for the same (pin, stage, attempt) and must not overwrite a first eligibility time; repair affected rows from the event log. Prevention: idempotent fold keyed by pin, stage and attempt, with tests that replay a day of events.

Follow-up guidance. Make them define the denominator (including deleted and stuck pins); push on queue time versus work time; ask how they would prove a change helped.

Rubric anchors. 2: one dashboard of median upload-to-impression for finished pins; timestamps from each service trusted. 3: stage events folded into an idempotent lifecycle table, eligibility separated from first impression, per-segment percentiles, stuck pins counted. 4: also a clock-consistent timeline with skew detection, censored-duration reporting, queue-versus-work breakdown driving fair queuing and autoscaling on queue age, before-and-after proof, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Separates what the pipeline controls from what the scoring function decides; worries about pins that never finish. Red flags. Skipping policy checks to meet the target; medians over finished pins only; double counting replays.

PIN-L5-01.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First hours: try to break the result. Check holdout integrity (assignment still random, sizes as expected, no leakage of the feature into the holdout, no change in who is logged), instrumentation (did the feature change what is logged, so the metric moves for a measurement reason?), duration (is the gap stable or still moving, novelty or learning effects), guardrails and related metrics (do saves, closeups and returning pinners tell a consistent story with {{metric}}?), and segments, without fishing for a segment that saves the feature. Ask a peer to review the analysis.
  • First day: tell the right people first. The product lead (the decision owner) and the feature's design and engineering leads, privately, before any wider forum, with the evidence, the uncertainty, and options: roll back, roll back part, change and re-test, or keep with an explicit cost. Never surprise the builders in a public meeting.
  • The decision: framed as the cost of keeping {{feature}} (the size of {{metric}} over a year, in terms the product lead values) against the cost of rolling back (work lost, public message, any pinners who prefer it). Respect that the product lead decides; give a clear recommendation and say what would change it.
  • Partial keep: if one part stays, test that part alone against the holdout (or re-run an experiment) instead of assuming it is the harmless part.
  • The team: separate the craft from the bet; credit what was built well and what was learned; make it safe to be wrong, because a team punished for negative results stops reporting them. Handle pushback on the data by inviting the sceptics into the analysis.
  • Next time: pre-registered primary and guardrail metrics, experiments long enough for novelty to fade, long-running holdouts for major launches, and a launch review that looks at guardrails.
  • Real example: a real time they brought unwelcome results about their own team's work, with what they checked, whom they told and how, what was decided, and what changed afterwards.

Red flags. Announcing the result broadly before checking it or before telling the builders; burying it because the team is proud; hunting for a segment that makes the feature look good; treating the rollback as their decision; blaming the designers.

Rubric anchors. 2: reports the number in a team meeting, or sits on it. 3: verifies the result, tells the decision owner and builders privately with options, respects decision rights, supports the team. 4: also rigorous checks (integrity, instrumentation, novelty, guardrails) without fishing, a quantified cost framing, a tested partial keep, concrete changes to launch practice, and a credible real example.

PIN-L5-02.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First weeks: listen and re-examine. Talk to designers one to one about what broke their trust; re-open the experiment that killed the earlier design, in the open, and say plainly if it was underpowered, stopped early or measured the wrong thing. Ask what the designers would accept as evidence of a good outcome.
  • Change your own side where justified. Retire misleading metrics; add measures closer to what designers care about (for example saves that are revisited later, board organisation after saving, return visits, outbound clicks that are not immediately bounced back), with their limits stated; add guardrails; pre-register experiments with designers, agreeing in advance what result would change whose mind.
  • Combine the evidence. Research explains why and generates hypotheses; experiments measure how much at scale. Around {{decision}}, lay out what each source says, where they agree, and what would resolve a disagreement (a targeted experiment, a follow-up research round on the specific behaviour). Keep research participants' sessions separate from usage data, as the constraints require.
  • Presenting contradicting evidence: to the designers first, with uncertainty, as a question about what explains the difference, not as proof they were wrong. The product lead decides with both cases presented fairly.
  • Signs trust is returning: designers bring questions to the data team early; they co-design experiments; they cite a metric in their own reviews.
  • Real example: a real team that distrusted their data, what they changed in their own methods, and how the relationship changed.

Red flags. "Data beats opinions"; treating designers as obstacles; refusing to re-examine the old experiment; joining research participants to their usage data; going to the product lead to win before working with the designers.

Rubric anchors. 2: tries to win the argument with more dashboards. 3: listens, re-examines the old case honestly, adjusts metrics, combines research and data around the decision. 4: also co-designed, pre-registered experiments, measures with stated limits for what designers value, careful handling of privacy limits, clear signs of rebuilt trust, and a credible real example.

PIN-L5-03.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First conversation: private, in their working hours, framed as "how is onboarding going, and what would have helped?" rather than as a concern. Ask about blockers (access, local setup, unclear ownership in {{area}}, conflicting review comments, who to ask), not about personal circumstances; listen more than talk.
  • Look for system causes: a team that started in an office shares context by overhearing; asynchronous reviews that arrive overnight across {{gap_hours}} hours and contradict each other multiply round trips; onboarding documents are stale; meetings are scheduled at the edge of their day. Treat these as the team's problems to fix.
  • Concrete help: a named onboarding buddy; pairing in the overlapping hours (rotating who shifts their day); a sequence of small, well-scoped changes with a single primary reviewer and agreed review turnaround; written context for {{area}} (architecture, data flows, owners, common failure modes, how to test); an early, shadowed on-call shift.
  • Feedback: specific, about the work, with examples and a clear next step ("this change mixed a refactor with a fix; splitting them would have halved the review"), and also about what is going well.
  • The manager: share observations and the changes made, agree who does what; performance concerns are the manager's to raise. Keep anything personal the engineer shares out of the conversation unless they choose to share it.
  • A month later: judged by concrete signals (time from first commit to merged change, review rounds per change, questions asked in channels, a first on-call shift completed) and by asking the engineer.
  • Team change: updated onboarding for remote hires, review norms, meeting times that respect the overlap, written decisions.
  • Real example: a real person they helped ramp up, what they did personally, what changed in the team, and the outcome.

Red flags. Diagnosing the person before asking; asking about personal life; treating it as a performance problem to escalate; taking over the manager's role; help that consists of "they can always ask me".

Rubric anchors. 2: tells them to speak up more, or reports to the manager. 3: asks first, finds concrete blockers, sets up a buddy, pairing and scoped work, gives specific feedback, coordinates with the manager. 4: also fixes the team's remote practices (reviews, documentation, meetings), measures progress with concrete signals, respects privacy and role boundaries, and a credible real example.

PIN-L5-04.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Measure the cost in four weeks. Incidents and metric corrections traced to {{debt}} from incident records (with root causes, not just triggers); time lost estimated by a light, short time study (engineers log a week of interruptions) cross-checked against ticket data, not only by survey; lead time for changes that touch the debt versus comparable changes elsewhere; on-call pages caused by it; concentration of knowledge as a risk (what happens if one of the people who understand it leaves); the delay it adds to one item in {{roadmap}}, estimated with the engineers who will build it.
  • Translate: present cost in the product side's units: weeks added to roadmap items, creator- or merchant-facing incidents, engineers' time as a share of capacity, and the risk with a rough likelihood and impact. Be conservative and show the method, so the numbers survive questioning.
  • Options: (a) the full {{ask}}, (b) an incremental path that pays down the debt where roadmap work touches it (strangler pattern, one consumer or a group of jobs at a time), (c) a minimum that removes the biggest risk first. Each with cost, payoff and what it delays.
  • Payoff measures defined in advance: lead time for changes in the area, incidents and corrections, on-call load, number of job variants or format versions remaining.
  • If no or half: pick the highest-value slice, tie it to the roadmap item, keep measuring, and come back with results; never quietly slow the roadmap to force the issue.
  • Real example: a real case with the evidence they gathered, which number moved the decision, and what happened afterwards.

Red flags. "It's obviously bad"; numbers that cannot be defended; insisting on a rewrite; holding the roadmap hostage; not measuring the payoff afterwards.

Rubric anchors. 2: appeals to engineering quality, no numbers. 3: measures incidents, time and lead time defensibly, presents options in product terms, defines payoff. 4: also connects cost to a specific roadmap item, quantifies risk honestly, offers an incremental path, handles a partial yes well, and a credible real example with the decisive number.

PIN-L5-05.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Overview: a clear problem statement, who depended on the system, real numbers (volumes per day, peak to average, data size, freshness targets, cost), the architecture at the right altitude, and the candidate's role.
  • Depth on the chosen angle: for the data model and keys, the entities, keys and why they were chosen, and how schema changes were handled; for the hardest failure, the symptom, the diagnosis path, the root cause, the fix and the prevention; for the decision to undo, the original reasoning, what changed or what was missed, and the cost of undoing it.
  • In the visual discovery setting with {{pinners}} of pinners and {{requirement}}: for catalogue changes within an hour, catalogue uploads as validated diffs with quarantine for suspicious changes and prices and stock resolved at serving time from a current offers store. For creator analytics agreeing with billing, one deduplicated event pipeline and one metric definition feeding both, with daily reconciliation and recorded adjustments. For secret boards, visibility carried as data in the change stream to every public surface, cache invalidation by key, and acknowledgement tracking against the deadline. For visual search logs without the photo, logging detected categories, crop coordinates on public pins, result ids and what the pinner did next, never the image or anything that could reconstruct it, with debugging done by replaying results rather than images. Ranking stays a given scoring function. Accept other sound answers that fit their system.
  • Honesty: what failed, what they would change, what was the team's versus theirs.

How to judge. Probe numbers (per day or total? peak?), alternatives considered, and one failure in detail. A candidate who owned only part of a system and says so precisely scores well; one who claims the whole system but cannot explain its keys or failure modes does not.

Red flags. Only buzzwords; numbers that change under questioning; no failure ever; cannot say what they personally did; claims about how a real visual discovery company's ranking, storage or catalogue systems work; designs that infer sensitive attributes about pinners.

Rubric anchors. 2: high-level description, vague numbers, no clear personal contribution. 3: clear framing with numbers, real depth on the chosen angle, honest failure story, a sensible approach to the requirement. 4: also alternatives with evidence, an incremental and correct path to the requirement with its costs stated, crisp separation of own and team contributions, and lessons that show changed practice.
